 DiscoverAirdrie readers weigh in as Alberta Time divides opinion
 Anna Ferensowicz, 
 DiscoverAirdrie.com | 
 Friday, Nov 13 2026, 7:16 AM 
 Share: 
 Copied! 
 Light glows through clouds above a darkened treeline. A new Angus Reid Institute survey finds Albertans divided over their preferred permanent time, nearly two weeks after the province ended seasonal clock changes. File photo / Discover Airdrie 
 Article continues below advertisement ↴ 
 Alberta's clocks are staying put, but a new survey finds more Albertans would prefer permanent standard time over the daylight saving time the province adopted. A DiscoverAirdrie poll has also drawn mixed reactions from readers.
 According to findings released Thursday by the Angus Reid Institute , 44 per cent of Alberta respondents who expressed a preference favoured permanent standard time, while 33 per cent preferred permanent daylight saving time. Another 23 per cent wanted to return to changing clocks twice a year.
 Related Stories:
 Get ready to do absolutely nothing: Alberta's clocks won't fall back Sunday 
 No turning back: Alberta's clocks stay put, but some Airdrie booking times are wrong 
 New Alberta report estimates wages needed to cover living costs 
 Asked separately whether ending seasonal clock changes was the right decision, 46 per cent of Alberta respondents said it was, while 34 per cent disagreed.
 That question was distinct from asking respondents which time arrangement they preferred: permanent standard time, permanent daylight saving time or changing clocks twice a year.
 Alberta adopted permanent Alberta Time (ABT) on Nov. 1, keeping the province on the equivalent of Mountain Daylight Time year-round. Residents will no longer turn their clocks forward in spring or back in fall.
 Under permanent standard time, sunrises and sunsets would occur an hour earlier by the clock than under Alberta's chosen system. The amount of daylight would remain the same.
 What DiscoverAirdrie readers think 
 A DiscoverAirdrie online poll asking readers for their verdict on the change had attracted 304 votes as of Thursday evening.
 Of those, 139 votes, or 46 per cent, went to "Finally! Stop messing with the clocks."
 Another 102 votes, or 34 per cent, went to "Absolutely not. Bring back standard time."
 The remaining votes were split among three lighter responses: 32 for "I genuinely couldn't care less," 19 for "Wait, what time is it?" and 12 for "Ask me when it's dark at breakfast."
 Comments on the accompanying Facebook post reflected similar differences.
 Several readers welcomed the end of seasonal clock changes, while others looked forward to later sunsets after work. One commenter noted that an early morning commute would be dark regardless.
 Darker winter mornings drew complaints, and some readers argued that Alberta should have adopted permanent Mountain Standard Time instead.
 One commenter welcomed the chance to try the new system before drawing conclusions. Others described practical frustrations, including disrupted schedules and difficulty getting a smartwatch to display the correct time.
 The voluntary poll is not representative of Airdrie residents' opinions. Its answer choices also mix reactions to ending seasonal clock changes with preferences for a particular permanent time.
 Preference for permanent daylight saving time falls 
 The share of Alberta respondents who preferred permanent daylight saving time fell from 47 per cent in March to 33 per cent in November, according to Angus Reid.
 An Angus Reid Institute survey shows the proportion of Alberta respondents favouring permanent daylight saving time fell from 47 per cent in March to 33 per cent in November, while preference for permanent standard time rose from 41 to 44 per cent. Undecided respondents are excluded from the comparison. Graphic / Angus Reid Institute 
 Albertans were also more divided over the new arrangement than respondents in British Columbia and Manitoba, which stopped changing their clocks this year.
 Asked separately how they felt about keeping their clocks unchanged, 42 per cent of Albertans said they liked or loved the arrangement, compared with 54 per cent in B.C. and 57 per cent in Manitoba.
 Another 32 per cent of Albertans surveyed said they disliked or hated it.
 The Alberta government says permanent Alberta Time is intended to reduce disruptions and make scheduling more predictable for families, businesses, schools and services.
 The province plans to monitor the transition and gather feedback after the first full year.
 Angus Reid surveyed 1,634 Canadian adults online between Nov. 3 and 6, including 165 Albertans. Responses were weighted to reflect the Canadian adult population.
 Airdrie had its own scheduling headaches 
 In response to an open-ended survey question, 65 per cent of Alberta respondents reported challenges or annoyances associated with not turning their clocks back.
 Among 283 respondents across Alberta, B.C. and Manitoba who reported difficulties, 42 per cent cited electronic devices that failed to adjust properly. Another 27 per cent reported problems with calendars, meetings or scheduling, while 28 per cent disliked the darker mornings.
 Devices that failed to adjust, darker mornings and scheduling problems were among the most common complaints reported in an Angus Reid Institute survey. The figures reflect 283 respondents across Alberta, British Columbia and Manitoba who reported difficulties, not Alberta respondents alone. Graphic / Angus Reid Institute 
 Airdrie encountered a similar technical problem ahead of the transition.
 In an Oct. 19 notice, the City of Airdrie warned that some recreation and arts programs and rental bookings scheduled after Nov. 1 were displaying incorrect start times in its myAIRDRIE registration system.
 The city warned that some activities could appear to begin an hour later than scheduled. The problem concerned how times appeared online, rather than a change to the activities themselves.
 At the time, municipal staff were working with the software provider to correct the problem.
 For residents whose devices still display an incorrect time, the provincial government recommends installing available software updates and checking automatic date, time and time-zone settings. Older devices may require manual adjustments.
 One clock-change habit worth keeping 
 The twice-yearly clock change may be gone, but fire safety campaigns have long used it as a reminder to check smoke and carbon monoxide alarms.
 In an Oct. 5 Facebook post during Fire Prevention Week, Airdrie Fire Chief Mike Pirie encouraged residents to test their smoke alarms, replace batteries as needed and check the age of their devices, which generally need replacing every 10 years.
 He also advised ensuring smoke alarms are installed on every level of the home and outside sleeping areas.
 Pirie wrote:
 "When did you last test your smoke alarms? Working smoke alarms provide an early warning when a fire occurs, giving everyone valuable time to get outside safely."
